To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the average dose of lung tissue in the human lung is 0.1-0.3% of the dose at the airway wall surface.

the detriment-weighted average dose to the human respiratory tract is 0.1 Gy per year for a 1000 Bq m(-3) (1.0 pCi l(-1)) exposure, and the corresponding detriment-weighted average bronchial dose is 0.4 Gy per year for the same exposure.

(i) the average lung dose is a useful parameter for relating lung cancer risk to radon exposure; (ii) the average lung is not the sum of individual average airway doses, but is derived after applying weighting scenarios; and (iii) the choice of weighting scenarios has a significant effect on the resulting average lung dose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of appropriate dose weighting parameters to derive a single value of the average lung dose for a given exposure scenario.
the development of a biologically based model to derive the average lung dose from cellular dose distributions.

the following issues: (1) the derivation of a dose conversion factor for lung cancer risk from radon progeny, (2) the development of a biologically based dosimetry model for radon progeny in the human lung, (3) the development of an airway generation-specific dosimetry model, (4) the derivation of an average lung dose for the human lung, and (5) the development of biological weighting parameters for the derivation of an appropriate detriment-weighted average dose
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
average lung dose is the most appropriate parameter for relating epidemiologically observed lung dose and risk.
average lung doses are not suitable for epidemiological investigations of lung cancer risk.
the average lung dose is not a single number but a weighted average of a wide range of individual target cell doses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the average lung dose is a very sensitive indicator of the risk from exposure to radon progeny.
the lung dose averaged over the whole lung volume is a good predictor of the risk for bronchogenic cancer.
, although the lung cancer risk per unit of average lung dose is independent of the choice of weighting scenario, the average lung dose is not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lung cancer risk per unit average lung dose is not necessarily the same for all individuals.
, for a given radon progenor exposure, a single value for detriment-weighted average dose cannot be derived.
the choice of weighting scenario is critical for the derivation of a single average lung dose which relates lung cancer risk to radon progeny inhalation exposure conditions.
